ghs.en: Anger remains, so I file a complaint to Touko.
ghs.assessment: 怒りのまま says the narrator complains while still angry. 'Anger remains, so' turns the state into an explicit cause, while English files a complaint with or against someone rather than 'to' them.

rows.jp: 「だいたいおまえは武道家のはしくれなんだから力仕事くらいできるだろうが！　カマトトぶりやがってもう底は見えてるんだよ！　すぺぺぺぺっ！」

ghs.en: Taichi: "Aren't you some leftover of a martial artist or something, you can do some physical labor too you know! I can see all through to the bottom of your feigned ignorance by the way! Ner-nernerner!"
ghs.assessment: 武道家のはしくれ means even a lowly or novice martial artist, not a leftover. カマトトぶる means to feign innocence, while 'some leftover of' and 'all through to the bottom' are not coherent English renderings.
ghs.remedy: Say that even a novice martial artist can handle physical work and that he sees through her feigned innocence.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Aren't you some leftover of a martial artist or something, you can do some physical labor too you know! I can see all through to the bottom of your feigned ignorance by the way! Ner-nernerner!"

rows.jp: 「……女の細腕に何させようってのよ。馬鹿じゃないの」

ghs.assessment: The English splices an exclamation onto 'what do you want ... to do' and then punctuates the following direct insult as a statement. The source contains two coherent challenges.
ghs.remedy: Use 'What are you trying to make these slender arms do? Are you stupid?'

highlights.text: Touko: "...what do you want a woman's thin arms to do! Aren't you stupid."

rows.jp: 冬子は雪だから優しくするとすぐトロトロとけるので、絶対甘い顔は見せないと決めた。
rows.en: Touko was snow: show her a little warmth and she would melt into a puddle. I resolved never to coddle her.

ghs.en: Touko, written with the kanji for Winter and Child, is snow; therefore, when treated warmly she soon melts into a sticky syrupy mess. That is why she decided to absolutely never show her sweet side.
ghs.assessment: The narrator decides that he must never show Tōko indulgence because she melts when treated gently. The English makes Tōko the one who decides never to show her sweet side, reversing the acting subject and the lesson drawn from the snow metaphor.
ghs.remedy: Say that because Tōko melts when treated gently, the narrator resolves never to go easy on her.

highlights.text: Touko, written with the kanji for Winter and Child, is snow; therefore, when treated warmly she soon melts into a sticky syrupy mess. That is why she decided to absolutely never show her sweet side.

ghs.assessment: The line asks whether her behavior violates the philosophy of iai. 'The philosophy of unsheathe-cut-sheathe of the Iai' is not grammatical English and replaces the discipline with an improvised procedure label.

rows.jp: 居合とは、人に斬られず人斬らず、己を責めて平らかの道……。
rows.en: Iaido was the path of peace: be cut by none, cut no one, and discipline oneself...

ghs.en: Iai is a peaceful way of self-criticism where no man is slain and is slain by no man...
ghs.assessment: 己を責めて describes disciplining or mastering oneself on a peaceful path. 'Self-criticism' reduces it to fault-finding, while the doubled passive obscures the balanced injunction neither to cut nor be cut.
ghs.remedy: Use 'Iai is a peaceful path: cut no one, be cut by no one, and discipline the self.'

highlights.text: Iai is a peaceful way of self-criticism where no man is slain and is slain by no man...

ghs.assessment: いっそもろとも threatens to take both of them down together rather than live in disgrace. 'This is better for all of us' turns mutual destruction into a beneficial collective outcome.
ghs.remedy: Use 'Rather than live in disgrace, I'll take us both down!'

highlights.text: Touko: "If a life of disgrace is what awaits, then this is better for all of us!"

ghs.en: Taichi: "You burned school textbooks! You are the First Emperor of the Qin dynasty! The Third Reich!"

highlights.text: Taichi: "You burned school textbooks! You are the First Emperor of the Qin dynasty! The Third Reich!"

rows.jp: 「でもベッドの下に押しやられていたから、いらないのかなって……それになんか俗っぽい本ばかりだったし……その……女の人のハダカとか……」

ghs.en: Touko: "But I thought that if you hide them under the bed, then you don't need them... and also... it seemed sort of like a vulgar book... with those... those women all naked..."
ghs.assessment: The books had merely been shoved under the bed; 'if you hide them' makes that an intentional recurring condition. The English also shifts the plural books to singular 'a vulgar book' and repeats demonstratives without stable agreement.
ghs.remedy: Use 'But they had been shoved under the bed, so I thought you didn't need them... And they were all such vulgar books... with naked women...'

highlights.text: Touko: "But I thought that if you hide them under the bed, then you don't need them... and also... it seemed sort of like a vulgar book... with those... those women all naked..."

ghs.en: Taichi: "I'm telling you, they were study books!"

ghs.remedy: Use 'That's exactly why I call them academic books!'

highlights.text: Taichi: "I'm telling you, they were study books!"

rows.jp: 「人間の根元たる美を肉体に求めずしてミロヴィーが語れるか！　自らの彫った彫像の娘に恋してしまったいにしえのフィギュアオタクのことでも学んで恥じるがいい！」
rows.en: “How can you speak of the Venus de Milo without seeking the beauty at the root of humanity in the flesh!? Learn of that ancient figure otaku who fell in love with the girl he sculpted, and be ashamed!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "Could you talk about the Venus de Milo without the pursuit of the human fundamental of beauty that is in the body?! Learn of the Bishoujo Figurine Otakus of ancient times, who fell in love with the girls they themselves sculpted, and be ashamed!"
ghs.assessment: The source invokes the singular ancient figure enthusiast who fell in love with a statue he carved. The English invents 'Bishoujo,' pluralizes both enthusiasts and girls, and leaves the Venus clause in broken syntax.
ghs.remedy: Use a grammatical line about seeking fundamental human beauty in the body, then tell her to learn from the ancient statue enthusiast who loved the woman he carved.

highlights.text: Taichi: "Could you talk about the Venus de Milo without the pursuit of the human fundamental of beauty that is in the body?! Learn of the Bishoujo Figurine Otakus of ancient times, who fell in love with the girls they themselves sculpted, and be ashamed!"

rows.jp: 「そしておまえは後悔するんだ。書物が自然発火する華氏４５１度の世界でな。つまり焦熱地獄に堕ちるってことだ！　学術書を焼くってのはそういうことだ！　人類の敵め！」
rows.en: “And you will regret this in the world of Fahrenheit 451, where books spontaneously combust. In other words, you'll fall into the burning hell! That's what it means to burn scholarly works! Enemy of humanity!”

ghs.en: Taichi: "And now you shall repent. In the world of 451 Fahrenheit, where books spontaneously combust! In other words you are to be condemned into the fires of hell! That is the reward for roasting books of learning! You damn enemy of mankind!"
ghs.assessment: The referenced title and temperature are Fahrenheit 451, not '451 Fahrenheit.' 後悔する says she will regret it, not repent, and 'condemned into' and 'roasting books' break the mock-serious argument's grammar and register.
ghs.remedy: Use 'And you'll regret it in the world of Fahrenheit 451, where books spontaneously combust. In other words, you'll fall into a scorching hell!'

highlights.text: Taichi: "And now you shall repent. In the world of 451 Fahrenheit, where books spontaneously combust! In other words you are to be condemned into the fires of hell! That is the reward for roasting books of learning! You damn enemy of mankind!"

rows.jp: この数字は、太一という名前からつけた。
rows.en: I had derived the number from the name Taichi.

ghs.en: This number is derived by my name, Taichi.
ghs.assessment: A number is derived 'from' a name, not 'by' it.
ghs.remedy: Use 'I derived this number from the name Taichi.'

highlights.text: This number is derived by my name, Taichi.

rows.jp: 太＝多い、ということで桁の上限である９９９。＋太一の一で１。
rows.en: Tai meant ‘many,’ so I took 999—the limit of three digits. Then came the ichi in Taichi: one.

ghs.en: The 'Ta' can be read as 'many', and the farthest ends of that would of course be 999. Plus the 'ichi' in Ta-ichi, that is 1.
ghs.assessment: 桁の上限 identifies 999 as the upper limit for the chosen digits. 'The farthest ends of that' is not meaningful English and obscures the numerical construction.
ghs.remedy: Use 'Ta means many, so I take the maximum for those digits: 999. Then the ichi in Taichi gives 1.'

highlights.text: The 'Ta' can be read as 'many', and the farthest ends of that would of course be 999. Plus the 'ichi' in Ta-ichi, that is 1.

ghs.assessment: The narrator says the riddle-like twist should make the code harder to crack than a birthday. 'Difficult to derive than from a birthday' uses a malformed comparison and the wrong object for deriving.
ghs.remedy: Use 'With that bit of wordplay mixed in, it should be harder to crack than a birthday.'

highlights.text: So much wit is mixed there, that it should be much more difficult to derive than from a birthday.
